faqs.question: How long does alcohol withdrawal last?

answer_blocks.text: For most people, acute alcohol withdrawal lasts about five to seven days. Symptoms usually start within 6 to 12 hours of the last drink, peak around 48 to 72 hours, then ease over the following days. Some people have lingering post-acute symptoms, such as poor sleep and low mood, for weeks or months.

faqs.question: Can alcohol withdrawal kill you?

answer_blocks.text: Yes, though it is uncommon with proper care. Severe alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium tremens, both of which can be fatal if untreated. This is why medically supervised detox is strongly recommended for anyone with a heavy or long-term drinking history.

faqs.question: When does alcohol withdrawal start?

answer_blocks.text: Symptoms usually begin 6 to 12 hours after the last drink, often overnight as blood alcohol falls. Early signs include anxiety, shaky hands, sweating, nausea, and trouble sleeping. Symptoms then tend to build over the first day or two.

faqs.question: What is delirium tremens?

answer_blocks.text: Delirium tremens (DTs) is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal. It usually starts 48 to 72 hours after the last drink and causes severe confusion, agitation, fever, a racing heart, and hallucinations. It affects roughly 3 to 5 percent of people in withdrawal and is a medical emergency.

faqs.question: Is it safe to detox from alcohol at home?

answer_blocks.text: For mild dependence, a doctor may support a monitored taper at home. For anyone with heavy or long-term drinking, a history of seizures or DTs, or other health problems, home detox is risky because dangerous symptoms can appear suddenly. Supervised detox is the safer choice.

faqs.question: What medications are used for alcohol withdrawal?

answer_blocks.text: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam or lorazepam are the first-line treatment, because they ease symptoms and prevent seizures and DTs. Thiamine protects the brain, and fluids correct dehydration. Medications like naltrexone or acamprosate may be added later to support ongoing sobriety.

faqs.question: Why do I shake during alcohol withdrawal?

answer_blocks.text: Tremors happen because the nervous system becomes overactive without alcohol. The brain adapted to alcohol’s calming effect by increasing its own stimulating activity, so when the alcohol is gone, that overactivity shows up as shaking, anxiety, and a racing heart.

faqs.question: What is the kindling effect in alcohol withdrawal?

answer_blocks.text: Kindling means each repeated withdrawal can be worse than the last. Every episode sensitizes the brain, so people who have detoxed several times may face faster, more severe symptoms, including a higher risk of seizures, even at the same level of drinking.

faqs.question: Can you have a seizure from alcohol withdrawal?

answer_blocks.text: Yes. Withdrawal seizures are most likely in the first 24 to 48 hours after the last drink. They can happen even in people who felt they were coping, which is one of the main reasons not to go through heavy alcohol withdrawal alone.

faqs.question: How much do you have to drink to go through withdrawal?

answer_blocks.text: There is no exact threshold, because it depends on the person, but withdrawal is linked to heavy, regular drinking over time rather than occasional use. People who drink daily for months or years are the ones most likely to become physically dependent and experience withdrawal.

faqs.question: What is post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS)?

answer_blocks.text: PAWS refers to symptoms that linger after acute withdrawal ends, such as disrupted sleep, mood swings, low energy, and cravings that come in waves. It can last weeks to months as the brain rebalances, and it is a common trigger for relapse if people are not prepared for it.

faqs.question: How is alcohol withdrawal different from a hangover?

answer_blocks.text: A hangover is the short-term aftermath of a single episode of drinking and fades within a day. Withdrawal happens in people who are physically dependent and appears when they cut back or stop. It lasts longer, follows a timeline, and can become dangerous, which a hangover does not.

answer_blocks.text: Often no. Rapid Access Addiction Medicine (RAAM) clinics are designed for walk-in or low-barrier access without a referral, and many withdrawal management services accept self-referrals. A quick call to a helpline or clinic can tell you exactly what your local options require.

answer_blocks.text: Using alcohol to manage withdrawal keeps the cycle going and makes it hard to know how severe things are getting. If symptoms are strong enough that you are considering this, it is a sign you need medical support rather than another drink. A clinician can ease symptoms safely with proper medication.

Alcohol Withdrawal: Timeline, Symptoms, and Detox in Canada
blocks.html: Alcohol Withdrawal: Timeline, Symptoms, and Detox in Canada

blocks.text: If you have decided to stop drinking, or you are watching someone you love try to stop, the first few days can be frightening. Alcohol withdrawal is not a matter of willpower or discomfort you simply push through. For people who have been drinking heavily for a long time, stopping suddenly can trigger seizures and a life-threatening condition called delirium tremens. That is the hard truth, and it is also the reason this guide exists. Withdrawal is manageable, and it is far safer when you understand what is coming and get the right medical support.

blocks.text: This is a plain-language walk through what alcohol withdrawal actually feels like, hour by hour and day by day, what the warning signs of a medical emergency look like, and how supervised detox works in Canada. It is written for people in Ontario and across the country who want honest information without the scare tactics or the false reassurance.

blocks.text: What Is Alcohol Withdrawal?
blocks.html: What Is Alcohol Withdrawal?

blocks.text: Alcohol withdrawal is the set of physical and psychological symptoms that appear when someone who drinks heavily and regularly cuts back or stops. The brain adapts to constant alcohol by ramping up its own stimulating chemistry. Remove the alcohol and that revved-up nervous system has nothing to balance it, so it swings into overdrive. Tremors, sweating, anxiety, a racing heart, and in serious cases seizures are the result.

The brain adapts to constant alcohol by ramping up its own stimulating chemistry. Remove the alcohol and that revved-up nervous system has nothing to balance it, so it swings into overdrive. Tremors, sweating, anxiety, a racing heart, and in serious cases seizures are the result.

blocks.text: Not everyone who drinks will go through withdrawal. It happens in people whose bodies have become physically dependent, usually after months or years of heavy daily drinking. The more someone drinks and the longer they have been doing it, the higher the risk of severe symptoms. If you are unsure whether your drinking has reached that point, our guide on whether you might be an alcoholic can help you think it through honestly.

blocks.text: Why Alcohol Withdrawal Can Be Dangerous
blocks.html: Why Alcohol Withdrawal Can Be Dangerous

blocks.text: Most people are surprised to learn that alcohol is one of only a few drugs where withdrawal itself can kill you. Opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely fatal on its own. Alcohol is different. The same nervous-system rebound that causes shakes and sweating can, at its worst, cause seizures and delirium tremens, both of which are medical emergencies. This is why quitting cold turkey at home after years of heavy drinking is a genuine risk rather than a badge of toughness. The effects and dangers of alcohol addiction reach well beyond the drinking itself.

blocks.text: Who Is Most at Risk of Severe Withdrawal
blocks.html: Who Is Most at Risk of Severe Withdrawal

blocks.text: Certain people are more likely to have a rough, dangerous withdrawal. Risk climbs with heavy daily drinking over years, older age, poor nutrition, and other health problems such as liver disease. A history of previous withdrawals matters a great deal too, because of something called kindling, which we will get to. Anyone who has had a withdrawal seizure or an episode of delirium tremens before should treat any future attempt to stop as a medical situation from the start.

blocks.text: Alcohol Withdrawal Symptoms
blocks.html: Alcohol Withdrawal Symptoms

blocks.text: Symptoms range from unpleasant but manageable to genuinely dangerous. They tend to build in stages, and the same person can move from mild to severe over a day or two, which is why steady monitoring matters so much.

blocks.text: Mild and Moderate Symptoms
blocks.html: Mild and Moderate Symptoms

blocks.text: The early symptoms are the ones most people recognize. They include anxiety and restlessness, shaky hands, sweating, headache, nausea, a fast or pounding heartbeat, trouble sleeping, and a low, irritable mood. Many people also feel a strong pull to drink again, simply because a drink makes all of it stop for a while. These symptoms are uncomfortable, but on their own they are not usually dangerous in an otherwise healthy person.

blocks.text: Severe Symptoms and Complications
blocks.html: Severe Symptoms and Complications

blocks.text: A smaller number of people develop serious complications. Alcoholic hallucinosis can cause someone to see, hear, or feel things that are not there while they are still otherwise alert. Withdrawal seizures can strike, most often in the first day or two. And delirium tremens, the most dangerous outcome, brings severe confusion, agitation, fever, a racing heart, and vivid hallucinations. Severe symptoms are the reason to be in a setting where medical help is immediately available.

blocks.text: The First 6 to 12 Hours
blocks.html: The First 6 to 12 Hours

blocks.text: Symptoms usually begin within about six to twelve hours of the last drink, often once blood alcohol starts to drop overnight. This is why many people wake up shaky and anxious. Hands tremble, the stomach turns, sweat comes easily, and sleep feels impossible. It is the body noticing that the alcohol it expected is not there.

blocks.text: 12 to 48 Hours
blocks.html: 12 to 48 Hours

blocks.text: Over the next day the nervous system gets louder. Heart rate and blood pressure climb, tremors get stronger, and anxiety can tip into agitation. This stretch, roughly 24 to 48 hours in, is when withdrawal seizures are most likely. A seizure can happen even in someone who felt they were coping, which is one more reason not to go through this stage alone.

blocks.text: Days 4 to 7 and Beyond
blocks.html: Days 4 to 7 and Beyond

blocks.text: By the fourth or fifth day, the acute physical symptoms have usually calmed down for most people. Sleep is often still poor and mood can stay flat, but the dangerous phase has generally passed. This is the point where the focus shifts from surviving withdrawal to building a real recovery plan, whether that means residential rehab or a structured outpatient program.

blocks.text: Post-Acute Withdrawal Syndrome (PAWS)
blocks.html: Post-Acute Withdrawal Syndrome (PAWS)

blocks.text: Some people notice that even after the shakes are gone, they do not feel like themselves for a while. Post-acute withdrawal syndrome describes lingering symptoms such as disrupted sleep, low or unstable mood, irritability, low energy, and cravings that come in waves. These can last weeks and sometimes months as the brain slowly rebalances. PAWS is a common reason people relapse well after detox, so it helps to expect it and to have a relapse prevention plan ready.

blocks.text: Delirium Tremens: The Most Dangerous Complication
blocks.html: Delirium Tremens: The Most Dangerous Complication

blocks.text: Delirium tremens, often shortened to DTs, is the most serious form of alcohol withdrawal. It usually begins two to three days after the last drink and can last several days. It brings severe confusion and disorientation, intense agitation, fever, a rapid heartbeat, heavy sweating, and vivid hallucinations. It develops in an estimated 3 to 5 percent of people going through alcohol withdrawal, and without treatment it can be fatal. With prompt hospital care, the outlook is far better. If you see confusion, fever, or hallucinations during withdrawal, treat it as an emergency and call for help.

blocks.text: What Makes Withdrawal Worse
blocks.html: What Makes Withdrawal Worse

blocks.text: A few things reliably turn a rough withdrawal into a dangerous one. The amount and length of drinking is the biggest factor. Poor nutrition and dehydration make everything harder, and long-term heavy drinkers are often low on thiamine, a vitamin the brain badly needs. Other medical conditions, especially liver disease, raise the stakes. Then there is kindling.

blocks.text: The Kindling Effect
blocks.html: The Kindling Effect

blocks.text: Kindling is the reason repeated attempts to quit can each be worse than the last. Every time the brain goes through withdrawal, it becomes a little more sensitized, so future withdrawals can arrive faster and hit harder, even if the person was drinking the same amount. Someone who has detoxed several times before is not starting from zero. They may be at higher risk of seizures and DTs than their drinking history alone would suggest, which is a strong argument for medical supervision rather than another solo attempt.

blocks.text: How Alcohol Withdrawal Is Treated
blocks.html: How Alcohol Withdrawal Is Treated

blocks.text: The good news is that alcohol withdrawal is very treatable. With the right medication and monitoring, even severe cases can be managed safely, and the frightening complications can usually be prevented rather than just reacted to.

blocks.text: Medically Supervised Detox
blocks.html: Medically Supervised Detox

blocks.text: The safest way to withdraw from alcohol is under medical supervision, either in a hospital, a withdrawal management facility, or a residential program with medical staff. Supervised medical detox means someone is checking your vital signs and symptoms regularly and can step in with medication before things escalate. For anyone with a heavy drinking history, previous seizures or DTs, or other health problems, this is the level of care to aim for. You can read more about how the detox process works at a detox centre and what to expect day to day.

blocks.text: Medications Used in Alcohol Withdrawal
blocks.html: Medications Used in Alcohol Withdrawal

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment for alcohol withdrawal. They calm the overactive nervous system, ease symptoms, and lower the risk of seizures and DTs. Long-acting options such as diazepam are among the most studied. Alongside them, thiamine is given to protect the brain from a serious complication called Wernicke’s encephalopathy, and fluids and other vitamins help the body recover. In some cases, medications like naltrexone or acamprosate are started later to support ongoing sobriety, though those are for maintaining recovery rather than managing the acute phase.

blocks.text: The CIWA-Ar Assessment
blocks.html: The CIWA-Ar Assessment

blocks.text: Clinicians often measure withdrawal with a tool called the CIWA-Ar, a ten-item scale that scores symptoms such as nausea, tremor, sweating, anxiety, agitation, and hallucinations. The score guides how much medication a person needs and how often, an approach known as symptom-triggered dosing. Canadian protocols, including guidance from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), use this kind of scoring so that treatment matches the severity in front of them rather than a one-size-fits-all dose. It is one of the clear advantages of choosing a supervised alcohol detox program.

blocks.text: Can You Detox From Alcohol at Home?
blocks.html: Can You Detox From Alcohol at Home?

blocks.text: For someone with mild dependence and no history of severe withdrawal, a doctor may support a carefully monitored taper. For anyone else, home detox carries real risk, because seizures and DTs can appear with little warning and move quickly. If cost or access is your worry, please do not let that push you into an unsafe solo attempt. There are options, and our guide on getting help when you cannot afford rehab covers several of them. The safest path is to talk to a doctor or a Rapid Access Addiction Medicine clinic before you stop.

blocks.text: Getting Help for Alcohol Withdrawal in Canada
blocks.html: Getting Help for Alcohol Withdrawal in Canada

blocks.text: If you are in Ontario or anywhere in Canada, help is closer than you might think. You can start by looking at alcohol and drug rehab centres in Ontario or, if you are in the city, rehabs in Toronto.

blocks.text: Alcohol Withdrawal and Alcohol Harm in Canada
blocks.html: Alcohol Withdrawal and Alcohol Harm in Canada

blocks.text: It is easy to think of alcohol as the safe, ordinary drug, the one everyone uses. The numbers tell a heavier story. According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information, about ten Canadians die in hospital every day from harm caused by substance use, and roughly three quarters of those deaths are linked to alcohol. In 2023 the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction released new national guidance concluding that no amount of alcohol is completely safe, and that risk to health begins to climb beyond a couple of drinks a week.

blocks.text: How to Support Someone Going Through Withdrawal
blocks.html: How to Support Someone Going Through Withdrawal

blocks.text: If it is your partner, parent, or friend going through this, your instinct to help is exactly right, and you can help most by steering toward medical care rather than trying to manage it at home. Encourage a call to a doctor or a RAAM clinic. Watch for the warning signs that mean an ambulance, which are confusion, a seizure, a high fever, or hallucinations. Keep them hydrated and calm in the meantime, and do not leave a heavy drinker alone during the first few days.

blocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Alcohol Withdrawal
blocks.html: Frequently Asked Questions About Alcohol Withdrawal

blocks.text: How long does alcohol withdrawal last?
blocks.html: How long does alcohol withdrawal last?

blocks.text: For most people, acute alcohol withdrawal lasts about five to seven days. Symptoms usually start within 6 to 12 hours of the last drink, peak around 48 to 72 hours, then ease over the following days. Some people have lingering post-acute symptoms, such as poor sleep and low mood, for weeks or months.

blocks.text: Can alcohol withdrawal kill you?
blocks.html: Can alcohol withdrawal kill you?

blocks.text: Yes, though it is uncommon with proper care. Severe alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium tremens, both of which can be fatal if untreated. This is why medically supervised detox is strongly recommended for anyone with a heavy or long-term drinking history.

blocks.text: When does alcohol withdrawal start?
blocks.html: When does alcohol withdrawal start?

blocks.text: Symptoms usually begin 6 to 12 hours after the last drink, often overnight as blood alcohol falls. Early signs include anxiety, shaky hands, sweating, nausea, and trouble sleeping. Symptoms then tend to build over the first day or two.

blocks.text: What is delirium tremens?
blocks.html: What is delirium tremens?

It usually starts 48 to 72 hours after the last drink and causes severe confusion, agitation, fever, a racing heart, and hallucinations. It affects roughly 3 to 5 percent of people in withdrawal and is a medical emergency.

blocks.html: Is it safe to detox from alcohol at home?

blocks.text: For mild dependence, a doctor may support a monitored taper at home. For anyone with heavy or long-term drinking, a history of seizures or DTs, or other health problems, home detox is risky because dangerous symptoms can appear suddenly. Supervised detox is the safer choice.

blocks.text: Why do I shake during alcohol withdrawal?
blocks.html: Why do I shake during alcohol withdrawal?

blocks.text: Tremors happen because the nervous system becomes overactive without alcohol. The brain adapted to alcohol’s calming effect by increasing its own stimulating activity, so when the alcohol is gone, that overactivity shows up as shaking, anxiety, and a racing heart.

blocks.text: What is the kindling effect in alcohol withdrawal?
blocks.html: What is the kindling effect in alcohol withdrawal?

blocks.text: Kindling means each repeated withdrawal can be worse than the last. Every episode sensitizes the brain, so people who have detoxed several times may face faster, more severe symptoms, including a higher risk of seizures, even at the same level of drinking.

blocks.text: Can you have a seizure from alcohol withdrawal?
blocks.html: Can you have a seizure from alcohol withdrawal?

blocks.text: Yes. Withdrawal seizures are most likely in the first 24 to 48 hours after the last drink. They can happen even in people who felt they were coping, which is one of the main reasons not to go through heavy alcohol withdrawal alone.

blocks.text: How much do you have to drink to go through withdrawal?
blocks.html: How much do you have to drink to go through withdrawal?

blocks.text: There is no exact threshold, because it depends on the person, but withdrawal is linked to heavy, regular drinking over time rather than occasional use. People who drink daily for months or years are the ones most likely to become physically dependent and experience withdrawal.

blocks.text: What is post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS)?
blocks.html: What is post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS)?

blocks.text: PAWS refers to symptoms that linger after acute withdrawal ends, such as disrupted sleep, mood swings, low energy, and cravings that come in waves. It can last weeks to months as the brain rebalances, and it is a common trigger for relapse if people are not prepared for it.

blocks.text: Does alcohol withdrawal cause anxiety and depression?
blocks.html: Does alcohol withdrawal cause anxiety and depression?

blocks.text: Very often, yes. Anxiety, irritability, and low mood are core parts of withdrawal and can continue into the post-acute phase. For some people these feelings reflect an underlying condition that alcohol was masking, which is where dual diagnosis treatment becomes important.

blocks.text: How is alcohol withdrawal different from a hangover?
blocks.html: How is alcohol withdrawal different from a hangover?

blocks.text: A hangover is the short-term aftermath of a single episode of drinking and fades within a day. Withdrawal happens in people who are physically dependent and appears when they cut back or stop. It lasts longer, follows a timeline, and can become dangerous, which a hangover does not.

blocks.text: Can I drink a little to ease withdrawal symptoms?
blocks.html: Can I drink a little to ease withdrawal symptoms?

blocks.text: Using alcohol to manage withdrawal keeps the cycle going and makes it hard to know how severe things are getting. If symptoms are strong enough that you are considering this, it is a sign you need medical support rather than another drink. A clinician can ease symptoms safely with proper medication.

blocks.text: A Final Word
blocks.html: A Final Word

blocks.text: Alcohol withdrawal is one of the few withdrawals that genuinely deserves your caution, and it is also one of the most manageable when you have the right help. If you take one thing from this guide, let it be this: you do not have to prove anything by toughing it out alone. A phone call to a clinic or a helpline can turn a dangerous few days into a safe, supported start to recovery. That first step is often the hardest, and it is also the one that changes everything.
